regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 55.9","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY looks unimpeachable until you notice the RBI's own forecast sits at 6.7% YoY — a 110bps gap that reflects the statistical distance between press-release GDP and ground-level GVA. PMI Composite at 55.9 and IIP at 8.0% YoY confirm expansion, but core sector growth slipping to 4.8% YoY (from 5.0%) while capacity utilisation rises to 77.4% of capacity signals that the goods economy is tightening without a commensurate output response. The quality of this growth is services-led and credit-fuelled — both of which are vulnerable to the rate environment.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 5.54% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"The headline CPI print of 5.54% YoY is doing the RBI a disservice: decompose it and the real problem is fuel at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) feeding into WPI at 9.92% YoY, with food at 7.74% YoY rising for two consecutive months. Core CPI at 3.9% YoY sits at only the 28th percentile — which is the one number the RBI can point to for its pause — but the inversion is this: if fuel and food stay elevated, core will not stay benign for long, because input costs transmit with a 2-3 quarter lag. The RBI's own inflation forecast has already moved from 4.6% to 5.1% YoY. The pause is increasingly a bet on mean reversion that the data does not yet support.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.4% YoY; CD ratio 81%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 19.4% YoY against deposit growth of 17.8% YoY — a 160bps divergence widening for two consecutive months — keeps the CD ratio at 81% (73rd percentile historically). The last time India sustained a CD ratio above 80% while the repo rate was being held was the pre-taper period of FY13-14; within 18 months, the system faced an emergency liquidity squeeze. Today's buffer is NBFC credit accelerating to 15.8% YoY and corporate bond issuance at ₹18,700 cr / month, but both increase wholesale funding dependency — precisely the channel that seizes first under stress. The RBI sees this; watch for risk-weight tightening on unsecured and NBFC-linked exposures.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is a hold, but the real rate calculus is deteriorating: with CPI at 5.54% YoY and rising, the ex-ante real rate is barely positive. The RBI's inflation forecast upgrade to 5.1% YoY signals internal discomfort that the communiqué underplays. Externally, the Fed at 3.75% p.a. and US 10Y at 5.1% yield compress India's carry advantage — the spread between repo and US 10Y is now only 15bps, the thinnest since the 2013 taper episode. A rate cut from here would be a gift to FII outflows; a hike would choke the capex cycle. The RBI is parked in a corridor with no clean exit.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY for a second consecutive month of acceleration, paired with capacity utilisation rising to 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile), is the most credible signal that the private investment cycle is real, not budgetary. The threshold that historically triggers broad-based private capex is 80% utilisation — at 77.4%, the economy is close but not there. Credit to industry at 18.2% YoY and credit to services at 24.3% YoY (rising two in a row) confirm that banks are funding the expansion. The risk: if deposit mobilisation falters and the RBI tightens macro-prudential conditions, credit to industry is the first tap to turn.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹203521 cr/mo; PV 7.9% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹2,03,521 cr / month is a record, but the composition matters: passenger vehicle sales have decelerated to 7.9% YoY for two consecutive months (from 26.1%), and commercial vehicle sales are falling at 12.6% YoY — the segment most sensitive to freight demand and rural income. Two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY are the one bright spot, and they are the informal economy's consumption signal. E-commerce GMV growth at 12.4% YoY sits at the 15th percentile — the weakest in a decade — suggesting that urban discretionary spend is being squeezed, likely by fuel costs absorbing wallet share. GST's record is partly formalisation; the vehicle and e-commerce data are the honest proxies.","badge_label":"Stable Consumption","badge_type":"b-neu"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.4% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 17.8% YoY — a 160bps divergence widening for 2 consecutive months (17.1%→19.4% credit; 9.9%→17.8% deposits). CD ratio at 81% credit÷deposits, down from 82.2% but still at 73rd percentile historically. NBFC credit accelerating at 15.8% YoY (up from 10% YoY), now at 57th percentile. Corporate bond issuance at ₹18,700 cr/month signals alternative funding, but wholesale dependency rising.","implication":"RBI will face pressure to either hike rates (to attract deposits) or tighten liquidity. Overweight private banks with CASA ratios >45% — they'll poach deposits from smaller lenders. Avoid NBFCs with wholesale funding >30% of liabilities; their funding costs will spike. Watch for RBI to signal deposit-friendly measures in next policy. Equity: Bank Nifty at 92nd percentile — take profits on strength.","pct_10y":73,"pct_note":"CD ratio at 73rd percentile is elevated but not crisis-level. Last time it breached 82% (2022), RBI tightened liquidity and rates rose 250bps over 6 months. Current divergence is structural — credit demand outpacing deposit mobilisation.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.2: {"signal_num":2,"signal_theme":"CAPEX TRIGGER","status":"positive","title":"Capex Upcycle Broadening, Capacity Tightening","data_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY (latest), up from 16.1% YoY — 2nd consecutive month of acceleration. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (up from 75.6%), now at 74th percentile. Core sector growth at 4.8% YoY (down from 5%), but this masks divergence: credit to industry at 18.2% YoY (up from 7%), credit to services at 24.3% YoY (rising 2 in a row). Vehicle credit at 19.7% YoY (up from 8.7%), agricultural credit at 17.2% YoY (up from 7.6%).","implication":"Capex cycle is broadening beyond traditional manufacturing into services and agri-tech. Overweight capital goods, auto ancillaries, and industrial equipment makers. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% leaves room for 3-5% more growth before bottleneck pricing kicks in — expect margin expansion for 12-18 months. Avoid over-leveraged capex plays; credit growth is strong but deposit stress may tighten lending standards by Q3.","pct_10y":74,"pct_note":"Capacity utilisation at 74th percentile is healthy mid-cycle. When it breaches 80%, pricing power emerges but capex ROI compresses. Current level suggests 18-24 months of productive investment ahead.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.3: {"signal_num":3,"signal_theme":"SIP / RETAIL FLOWS","status":"positive","title":"SIP Momentum Intact, But Ticket Size Rising","data_text":"SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr/month (latest), rising 3 consecutive months (₹29,845→₹31,961→₹32,297→₹32,490). SIP accounts at 10.06 mn (down from 10.45 mn), but SIP AUM at ₹17.86 lakh cr (up from ₹16.64 lakh cr over same period). SIP YoY growth at 10.7% (down from 15% a quarter ago), but equity MF net inflows at ₹38,307 cr/month (up from ₹29,329 cr/month). DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr/month (95th percentile), offsetting FII outflows of ₹49,935 cr/month.","implication":"Retail is rotating from mass SIP (account growth stalling) to larger ticket sizes — affluent money entering late-cycle. This is a warning signal: SIP growth deceleration + rising AUM per account = late-stage retail participation. Maintain overweight on quality large-caps; avoid micro-cap SIP darlings. DII strength is masking FII weakness — watch for reversal if global rates stay elevated. Nifty 50 at 74th percentile; take tactical profits on 5-7% rallies.","pct_10y":93,"pct_note":"SIP inflows at 93rd percentile are near all-time highs, but account growth stalling is a classic late-cycle signal. In 2021, SIP AUM surged while accounts plateaued — market peaked 6 months later.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.4: {"signal_num":4,"signal_theme":"OIL / COMMODITY RISK","status":"risk","title":"Fuel Inflation Spike Threatens RBI's Pause","data_text":"Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (latest), up from 20.05% YoY — 95th percentile historically. Brent crude at $108.66/bbl (75th percentile), WTI at $98.13/bbl (81st percentile). FAO food index at 136 (61st percentile), up from 134.5. CPI headline at 5.54% YoY (up from 4.83%), core CPI at 3.9% YoY (28th percentile, but rising). Food inflation at 7.74% YoY (rising 2 in a row). RBI inflation forecast at 5.1% YoY (up from 4.6%), repo rate held at 5.25% p.a.","implication":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile is a structural headwind RBI cannot ignore. If Brent stays >$105/bbl for 2 more months, RBI will be forced to hike despite growth concerns — repo rate to 5.50-5.75% by Q2. Overweight energy stocks (IOC, BPCL) and underweight consumer discretionary. Hedge INR weakness (see Sig6). Avoid long-duration bonds; 10Y Treasury at 5.1% yield (92nd percentile) is a ceiling, not a floor.","pct_10y":95,"pct_note":"Fuel inflation at 95th percentile last occurred in 2022 (pre-rate hike cycle). RBI tolerated it for 2 months before acting. Current pause is data-dependent; next CPI print (if >5.5%) will trigger hawkish pivot.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.5: {"signal_num":5,"signal_theme":"GLOBAL LIQUIDITY","status":"risk","title":"Fed Pause Masking Tightening Bias Globally","data_text":"Fed funds rate at 3.75% p.a. (up from 3.63%), 68th percentile, rising 2 in a row. US CPI at 3.72% YoY (rising 3 in a row), core CPI at 2.57% YoY. US 10Y Treasury at 5.1% yield (down from 5.19%, but 92nd percentile). ECB deposit rate at 2.5% p.a. (rising 2 in a row), BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, rising 2 in a row). US PMI composite at 58.4 index (91st percentile, rising 2 in a row). Global PMI composite at 54.3 index (84th percentile). DXY at 101.88 (55th percentile).","implication":"Fed is on pause but inflation is re-accelerating (CPI rising 3 in a row). BOJ tightening at 100th percentile is a structural headwind to carry trades — yen strength will pressure INR. ECB staying hawkish (2.5% deposit rate) keeps EUR bid. US PMI at 91st percentile signals no recession — expect Fed to skip rate cuts through 2026. Reduce leverage; unwind carry trades. Overweight USD and JPY; underweight INR and emerging market currencies. Avoid long-duration global bonds.","pct_10y":92,"pct_note":"US 10Y at 92nd percentile is a structural ceiling. Last time it was here (2022), it stayed elevated for 18 months. BOJ at 100th percentile is unprecedented — yen carry unwind will be violent if it accelerates.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.6: {"signal_num":6,"signal_theme":"INR / FX RESERVES","status":"risk","title":"INR Weakening Despite Strong Domestic Flows","data_text":"INR at 95.24 ₹/USD (up from 94.95), 89th percentile, rising 2 of last 5 periods. DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr/month (95th percentile), but FII equity net at -₹49,935 cr/month (17th percentile). SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr/month (93rd percentile), yet INR still weakening. Gold in INR at ₹12,863/g (100th percentile, up from ₹12,764). US 10Y Treasury at 5.1% yield (92nd percentile) vs RBI repo at 5.25% p.a. — carry trade incentive collapsing.","implication":"INR weakness despite strong domestic retail flows signals FII outflows are structural, not cyclical. RBI is likely intervening to slow depreciation (INR at 89th percentile is near intervention threshold). If US 10Y stays >5.1%, FII outflows will accelerate — INR could breach 96.50 by Q2. Overweight USD hedges; avoid unhedged USD exposure. Reduce INR-denominated bond duration. Watch RBI's FX reserve drawdown — if it exceeds $2bn/month, RBI is in defensive mode. Equity: Avoid large-cap exporters; overweight domestic-focused plays.","pct_10y":89,"pct_note":"INR at 89th percentile is near RBI's historical intervention zone (95.50-96.00). Last time it weakened this fast (2022), RBI burned $15bn in reserves over 3 months before stabilising.","is_surprise":false}
signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Collapse Signals GCC Shift, Not IT Weakness","data_text":"Office absorption at 4.0 mn sq ft/quarter (latest), down from 5.3 mn sq ft/quarter — 0th percentile (lowest on record). Office vacancy at 14.37% vacant (up from 13.74%), 41st percentile. Yet Nifty IT is flat (recent: 22,520→23,146, +2.8% over 5 periods), and India credit to services at 24.3% YoY (rising 2 in a row, 79th percentile). Rent in Bengaluru at ₹109/sqft/mo (up from ₹100.6), Mumbai at ₹156/sqft/mo (up from ₹125) — both rising despite absorption collapse. Retail mall vacancy at 4.8% vacant (down from 5%), 7th percentile (tightest on record).","implication":"Office absorption collapse is NOT an IT services crisis — it's a structural shift to Global Capability Centers (GCCs) and hybrid work. GCCs occupy smaller, premium spaces (hence rent rising despite absorption falling). Traditional IT services are consolidating real estate while services credit grows 24% YoY — this is capex reallocation, not demand destruction. Retail mall tightness (4.8% vacancy, 7th percentile) signals consumer discretionary is thriving. Implication: Overweight consumer discretionary and GCC-adjacent IT (Infosys, TCS capex plays). Avoid traditional IT outsourcing plays. Commercial RE REITs (Embassy, Mindspace) are pricing in office doom — they're oversold; retail REITs are the real opportunity. Falsifiable: If office absorption stays <5 mn sq ft/quarter for 3 more quarters AND Nifty IT underperforms by >10%, thesis breaks.","pct_10y":7,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 7th percentile is a 10-year low, but this coincides with retail vacancy at 7th percentile (tightest ever) — a bifurcation. In 2020-21, both fell together (COVID). Today's divergence suggests structural reallocation, not cyclical weakness. Last time office and retail diverged this sharply (2015-16), it preceded a 3-year commercial RE repricing.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

7.8% GDP, But the Consumption Engine Is Losing Torque

The facts:

  • GDP at 7.8% YoY and PMI Composite at 55.9 signal expansion — but the RBI's own forecast of 6.7% YoY implies a 110bps statistical gap between headline and ground-level output.
  • IIP Capital Goods at 16.9% YoY (second consecutive month of acceleration) and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity confirm the investment cycle is real.
  • But e-commerce GMV growth at 12.4% YoY (15th percentile, 10-year low) and passenger vehicle sales decelerating to 7.9% YoY for two consecutive months signal urban discretionary demand is fading.
  • Two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY — the informal economy's consumption barometer — remain the lone consumption bright spot, masking weakness in the formal demand chain.

The tension: The investment cycle and the consumption cycle are diverging: capex indicators are at multi-year highs while the discretionary demand proxies that fund corporate earnings growth are softening. A capex upcycle without consumption follow-through stalls at the revenue line.

Bottom line: Watch passenger vehicle sales: a third consecutive month below 10% YoY would confirm consumption deceleration is structural, not seasonal, and would pressure consumer discretionary earnings estimates.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

DM Re-acceleration Narrative Meets a 92nd-Percentile Bond Market

The facts:

  • US PMI Composite at 58.4 (91st percentile, rising two in a row) and Global PMI Composite at 54.3 (84th percentile) signal DM re-acceleration.
  • But US 10Y Treasury at 5.1% yield (92nd percentile) is doing the Fed's tightening for it — real economy stress is embedded in the curve, not the survey.
  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile, rising two in a row) is the underappreciated tail: every 25bps of BOJ normalisation unwinds yen carry trades that have funded EM equity inflows since 2021.
  • Eurozone CPI at 3.8% YoY (rising two in a row) with ECB deposit rate at 2.5% p.a. (rising two in a row) means European tightening is not done — a second front of global liquidity withdrawal.

The tension: Survey-based growth indicators are pricing re-acceleration; bond markets and central bank rate paths are pricing sustained tightening. One of them is wrong, and the bond market has a better track record of being right first.

Bottom line: BOJ's next meeting is the single most important global liquidity event for India — a 25bps hike from 1.25% p.a. would accelerate yen carry unwind and amplify FII outflows already running at ₹49,935 cr / month.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

SIP Autopilot Holds the Market — But the Fuel Tank Is Narrowing

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (93rd percentile, rising three consecutive months) are absorbing FII equity outflows of ₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile) — but DII net at ₹51,829 cr / month is only just covering the gap.
  • SIP accounts fell to 10.06 mn from 10.45 mn, while SIP AUM rose to ₹17.86 lakh cr — fewer accounts, larger tickets, meaning concentration risk in the retail base is rising.
  • NFO collections at ₹998 cr / month (2nd percentile, 10-year low) signal that institutional product demand has dried up — the smart-money distribution channel is closed.
  • But INR at 95.24 ₹/USD (89th percentile) is weakening despite record DII support — the currency is telling a different story than the equity market.

The tension: Domestic liquidity is mechanically supporting equities through SIP inflows, but the structural signals — falling SIP account counts, collapsed NFO demand, and a weakening rupee despite strong DII flows — suggest the support is narrowing, not broadening.

Bottom line: If SIP inflow growth (currently 10.7% YoY, down from 15% a quarter ago) drops below 8% YoY, the DII buffer against FII outflows compresses materially — watch the November SIP print.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

NRI Demand Holds Premium; Office REITs Price the Absorption Collapse

The facts:

  • NRI residential buying is RISING — NRI share of purchases at 20% (up from 10%, +10 pp), with 25% share within premium/luxury; remittances at $73 bn (12.8% YoY) provide the funding runway.
  • Hyderabad leads city momentum with sales +15% YoY and launches +120% YoY, but 28 months of unsold inventory is a supply overhang that NRI demand alone cannot clear.
  • Office absorption at 4.0 mn sq ft / quarter (0th percentile — lowest on record) has not stopped Bengaluru rents rising to ₹109/sqft/mo and Mumbai to ₹156/sqft/mo — GCC occupiers (41% of leasing) are taking less space but paying more for it.
  • But Embassy REIT at ₹370/unit, Mindspace at ₹345/unit, and Brookfield at ₹263/unit are all down sharply from prior levels — the listed market has already priced the absorption collapse that the rental data has not yet confirmed.

The tension: Physical office rents are rising while listed REIT units are falling — either the rental market is lagging the demand destruction, or REIT unit prices are overshooting the absorption signal. The GCC-driven occupier mix (41%) is the swing factor.

Bottom line: Avoid office REITs until absorption recovers above 8 mn sq ft / quarter; overweight residential developers with NRI-facing premium inventory in Hyderabad and Bengaluru.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Four Fuses, One Detonator — Fuel Inflation Is Lighting Them All

The facts:

  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile, rising) — every sustained quarter at this level adds ~40bps to headline CPI and forces the RBI to abandon its pause narrative.
  • FII equity outflows at ₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile) with INR at 95.24 ₹/USD (89th percentile) — carry compression from US 10Y at 5.1% yield makes further outflows the path of least resistance.
  • CD ratio at 81% (73rd percentile) with credit growing at 19.4% YoY vs deposits at 17.8% YoY — a macro-prudential tightening circular on NBFC or unsecured lending would reprice the credit cycle abruptly.
  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile) — a further hike accelerates yen carry unwind, amplifying FII outflows and INR depreciation simultaneously.

The tension: Each risk is individually manageable; the danger is sequencing — fuel inflation forces RBI hawkishness, which compresses growth, which widens the fiscal deficit, which pressures INR, which amplifies FII outflows, which the DII buffer may no longer fully absorb.

Bottom line: Watch the October CPI print (due ~12 Nov): a second consecutive month above 5.5% YoY would close the door on any rate cut and open the debate on a hike — the threshold that reprices every asset class simultaneously.

"}
